title: Inference and the network
lead: The net engine combines two parts: a small neural network that judges a position at a glance, and a Monte Carlo Tree Search that decides where to look next. This page follows one board from its encoding as numbers through the layers of the network to the move that the search picks, and shows where that computation runs.

sec.why-mcts.title: Why a tree search with a network
sec.why-mcts.p1: The classical engine of {sec:classical/alpha-beta|topic 2} searches every move to a fixed depth and judges the final positions with a formula. {term:mcts|Monte Carlo Tree Search} (MCTS) works differently: it grows the {term:game-tree|game tree} one path at a time and sends more paths down the moves that look promising. One path from the root to a new position is one {term:simulation}. Per move, the search keeps a visit count and an average result, much like a `HashMap` from move to statistics, and finally plays the most visited move.
sec.why-mcts.p2: Textbook MCTS judges a new position by playing random moves until the game ends. In this game that fails: pieces may move backwards, so a random game has no bound on its length and practically never ends ({src:docs/search-and-evaluation.md}, reported there from the literature). The project therefore follows AlphaZero. A {term:neural-network|neural network} judges each new position directly, and it also says which moves deserve a look first.
sec.why-mcts.p3: The net engines are an option, not the default: the browser starts with the classical alpha-beta engine, and you pick a net engine in the engine sheet. On one JVM thread, one simulation costs about {n:0.29} ms, while one {term:node} of the strongest classical search costs about 0.0008 ms. One simulation is worth 120 to 230 classical nodes, so at equal CPU time the classical search stays a little ahead.
sec.network-basics.title: A neural network in Java terms
sec.network-basics.p1: For a Java developer, a {term:neural-network|neural network} is best seen as a pure function: positions in, numbers out. Its behaviour is set by about {n:62000} numbers, the {term:parameters}, not by `if` statements. The code of the function never changes. Training only adjusts those numbers until the outputs fit many example positions; {sec:training/overview|topic 4} shows how. Running the function with fixed numbers is called {term:inference}, and one run is a {term:forward-pass|forward pass}. A game only ever does inference. Training costs about three times the work of a forward pass per example.
sec.network-basics.p2: The data travel as {term:tensor|tensors}. A tensor is a multi-dimensional array with a shape; in this project it is always a flat `float[]` plus that shape. The board becomes a tensor of shape `[122][13]`: one row per cell, plus one padding row, and 13 numbers per row. The element at (row, channel) sits at index `row · C + channel`, the same way you would flatten a matrix by hand. Each number in a row belongs to a {term:channel}: one property of that cell, like one column of a table row.
sec.network-basics.p3: The network is a stack of {term:layer|layers}. Each layer takes a tensor and returns a new one: it multiplies by a matrix of {term:weights-bias|weights}, adds a bias vector, and applies a simple non-linear {term:activation-function|activation function}. Without that last step, the whole stack would collapse into one single matrix multiplication and could only learn straight-line relationships. The shipped models are small: the expert model has {n:61734} parameters, about 240 KB as 32-bit floats.
sec.encoding.title: The board as numbers
sec.encoding.p1: Before the network sees a position, the encoder turns it into {term:input-plane|input planes} ({src:nn/src/main/java/sternhalma/nn/Encoder.java}). A plane is one channel that the code computes, with one value per cell. Plane 0 holds 1 where the player to move has a piece and 0 elsewhere; planes 1 and 2 do the same for the other players. Further planes mark the mover's goal corner, start corner and the cells the mover may stand on. Plane 6 holds the progress of the game, the current ply divided by the move limit, in every cell.
sec.encoding.p2: The shipped expert model reads 13 planes, the plane set `classic1` ({src:nn/src/main/java/sternhalma/nn/PlaneSet.java}). Planes 7 to 12 hand the network what the classical engine already knows: the distance of each side to its goal, the cells each side reaches in one move, whether the armies have passed each other, and the score of the {sec:classical/evaluation|linear evaluation}. The network does not have to rediscover these facts from bare piece positions. The shared model for all four variants adds two planes: one for the long hop and one for three players.
sec.encoding.p3: The encoder also rotates the board. The network always sees it as if the player to move had started in the top corner: rotated by 180° for the second of two players, and by 120° in either direction for the other players in a three-player game ({src:nn/src/main/java/sternhalma/nn/Orientation.java}). The same rotation maps both cells of every move. This {term:canonical-orientation|canonical orientation} lets one set of weights serve every seat at the table.
sec.hex-conv.title: Convolution on a star
sec.hex-conv.p1: Image networks use a {term:convolution}: the same small weight matrix is applied at every pixel to that pixel and its neighbours. It finds a local pattern, such as an edge, wherever the pattern occurs. A board game needs the same idea, because a piece that can jump is worth noticing anywhere on the board. The usual square-grid convolution does not fit a star-shaped board on which a cell has up to six neighbours, so the project uses its own {term:hex-convolution|hex convolution}.
sec.hex-conv.p2: It works in two steps ({src:nn/src/main/java/sternhalma/nn/HexGrid.java}). First a gather: for each of the 121 cells, copy the channels of the cell and of its 6 neighbours into one vector of `7 · C_in` values. The neighbours come from a precomputed `int[121][7]` table, much like a join against a neighbour table. A neighbour off the board points at the padding row 121, which holds only zeros. Second, multiply that vector by a weight matrix of shape `[C_out][7 · C_in]` and add a bias. The figure below shows the gather on the board.
sec.hex-conv.p3: Not every cell has 6 neighbours on the board. Of the 121 cells, 73 (about 60 %) have 6, 6 have 5, 36 have 4, and the 6 corner tips have only 2. The padding row keeps the code free of special cases: every cell gathers exactly 7 entries, and a missing neighbour adds zeros. What remains is a plain matrix-vector product per cell, the operation that CPUs, {term:simd|SIMD} units and GPUs all do well.
sec.trunk-heads.title: Trunk, heads and priors
sec.trunk-heads.p1: The network has a shared {term:trunk-heads|trunk} and two heads ({src:nn/src/main/java/sternhalma/nn/Network.java}). The trunk starts with one hex convolution from 13 input planes to 32 channels, followed by 4 {term:residual-block|residual blocks}. A residual block runs two hex convolutions and adds its own input back: `ReLU(conv2(ReLU(conv1(x))) + x)`. Each block therefore only has to learn a correction to what it receives, which keeps deeper stacks trainable. The activation is {term:relu|ReLU}, `max(0, x)`. Only standard operations are allowed (gather, matrix multiplication, bias, ReLU, addition, mean, tanh), so that every backend can implement them.
sec.trunk-heads.p2: The {term:policy} head turns the output of the trunk into two numbers per cell: a “from” {term:logit} and a “to” logit. A logit is a raw score, any real number; higher means more likely. The logit of a move is the from-logit of its start cell plus the to-logit of its target cell. A {term:softmax} over the legal moves turns these logits into probabilities that sum to 1, the {term:prior|priors}. Illegal moves are never scored, so no mask is needed. The price of this compact design: a sum of two per-cell scores cannot express every preference over pairs of cells.
sec.trunk-heads.p3: The {term:value} head averages the trunk over all 121 cells, passes the 32 averages through a dense layer of 32 and a second dense layer with one output per player, and squashes each output with {term:tanh} into the range −1 to +1: −1 is a certain loss, +1 a certain win. Two learned numbers add a classical prior ({src:nn/src/main/java/sternhalma/nn/ResidualPriors.java}): the move logit gains `beta · distance gain`, and the value gains `k · eval` before the tanh. Because `beta` starts at 1, `k` at 0.5 and both output layers at zero, an untrained network plays exactly the classical prior.
sec.forward-pass.title: One forward pass
sec.forward-pass.p1: The figure below runs the shipped expert model on three real positions: the start, a mid-game position after 30 plies, and a race position from a real game in which the armies have passed each other. Step through the layers. At the input you pick one of the 13 planes. For each later layer, the board shows how strongly each cell is activated across its 32 channels. At the end you see the five legal moves with the highest priors and the value for each player.
sec.forward-pass.p2: One forward pass of the SMALL network costs about 14 million {term:flop|floating-point operations} per position. The figure data come from the scalar Java reference `Network` ({src:nn/src/main/java/sternhalma/nn/Network.java}), with the F16 weights widened to F32 as the browser does. The reference adds up in `double` and in a fixed order. It is the oracle: every fast path is tested against it with a fixed tolerance, because a fast path may add in another order and in `float`.
sec.forward-pass.p3: A toggle switches between the final priors and the network's own logits without the residual priors; both were computed in advance. The difference shows how much of a move's prior comes from the classical distance gain and how much the network has learned on top of it.
sec.mcts.title: One MCTS simulation
sec.mcts.p1: One simulation has four steps ({src:search/src/main/java/sternhalma/search/Mcts.java}). Selection: from the root, each position follows the move with the highest {term:puct|PUCT} score. Expansion: the walk stops at a move whose resulting position is not in the tree yet. Evaluation: the network judges that new position and returns the priors of its legal moves and a value per player. Backup: every move on the path adds the value of the player who made it, and its {term:visit-count|visit count} grows by one. If the game is over there, the exact result replaces the network.
sec.mcts.p2: The PUCT score of a move is `Q + c · P · sqrt(N_parent) / (1 + N)` ({src:search/src/main/java/sternhalma/search/MctsNode.java}). Q is the average result of the move so far, P its prior, N its visit count, and N_parent the visits of the position above. The first term rewards moves that have worked, the second moves that the network likes and the search has rarely tried. The constant `c` sets the balance. N_parent counts as at least 1, so the priors decide which move a new position tries first.
sec.mcts.p3: Values are stored per player and never change sign, so the same code serves two and three players. After the last simulation the engine plays the most visited move. In the browser, the net engines run 50, 200 or 800 simulations with `c` = {n:1.0} ({src:teavm-net/src/main/java/sternhalma/webnet/WebNetCore.java}). Against the classical engine, `c` = {n:1.0} measured best at +338 ± 70 {term:elo|Elo}, but the results were flat between {n:0.5} and {n:1.5}; {sec:tuning/sweeps|topic 5} shows the sweep. {term:dirichlet-noise|Dirichlet noise} on the root priors makes self-play explore; in play it is off.
sec.backends.title: Where the forward pass runs
sec.backends.p1: The search and the forward pass are separate. The search is always the Java class `Mcts`; in the browser it runs compiled by {term:teavm|TeaVM} ({src:teavm-net/src/main/java/sternhalma/webnet/WebNet.java}). The forward pass sits behind a small interface, `NetBackend` with `load`, `evaluate` and `dispose` ({src:web/src/engines/net/backend.ts}). There are five {term:backend|backends}: the Java scalar reference, Java with the {term:vector-api|Vector API}, {term:tornadovm|TornadoVM} on a GPU for the server and for training, C++ compiled to {term:wasm|WebAssembly} for the browser CPU, and {term:wgsl|WGSL} shaders on {term:webgpu|WebGPU} for the browser GPU.
sec.backends.p2: Measured on one Apple M3 Max with the SMALL network and one position per call: the scalar reference reaches 115 evaluations per second and the Vector API {n:1760}, both on a loaded machine; under lower load the Vector API reached {n:2949}. In the browser, C++ WebAssembly reaches about {n:3100} with 128-bit SIMD and about {n:4000} with relaxed SIMD. The same Java network compiled by TeaVM reaches only 126 to 163, which is why the browser computes the forward pass in C++ and keeps only the search in Java.
sec.backends.p3: A GPU needs many positions per call. TornadoVM on the M3 Max manages {n:1968} evaluations per second one at a time, but {n:111409} with {term:batch|batches} of 256. MCTS pays for batches with strength: to fill a batch, the search picks several leaves before it knows any of their results, and a {term:virtual-loss|virtual loss} only spreads them over different paths. Against a classical engine with 400 nodes, a batch of 64 dropped the net engine from +542 ± 136 to +85 ± 43 Elo. The shipped code therefore uses {term:leaf-batching|leaf batches} of 1 on the CPU and 4 or 8 on WebGPU. Large batches come from parallel self-play games ({sec:training/throughput|topic 4}).
sec.model-files.title: Model files
sec.model-files.p1: A trained network is stored as a {term:safetensors} file: 8 bytes for the header length, a JSON header with the names and shapes of the tensors and metadata such as channels, blocks and plane set, then the raw numbers ({src:nn/src/main/java/sternhalma/nn/Safetensors.java}). The browser ships two models, an expert for two players and a shared model for all four variants, listed in {src:web/models/models.json}. Each file is about 115 KB and sits in plain git, not in Git LFS.
sec.model-files.p2: The weights are stored as {term:f32-f16|F16}, 16-bit floats, and compressed with gzip ({src:scripts/models/pack-model.py}); the browser widens them back to F32 before it computes. For the expert model this turns {n:249384} bytes into {n:114957} (about 46 %). gzip alone would save only about 8 %, because the bits of floats look almost random to it. This is the project's only {term:quantization}. On {n:2000} test positions, the F16 expert picked the same best move as the F32 original in all {n:2000} (100 %); the mean {term:kl-divergence|KL divergence} between the priors was 3 × 10⁻⁷ to 5 × 10⁻⁷ for the two models.
sec.model-files.p3: Before a model is used, the loader checks the download length and its SHA-256, the length and SHA-256 after inflating, and the safetensors header against the manifest ({src:web/src/engines/net/models.ts}). If any check fails, the engine shows a warning and plays random legal moves. The next topic, {sec:training/overview|training}, explains where these weights come from.

fig.net.title: The layers of the network
fig.net.desc: A vertical stack of the nine parts of the shipped network, from the input planes through the input convolution and four residual blocks to the policy head, the value head and the two residual priors, each with its output shape and parameter count. Beside it, a board shows which neighbours one cell gathers for a hex convolution.
fig.net.caption: Shapes and parameter counts come from the shipped model files. Pick a cell on the board: its convolution reads the cell and its 6 neighbours, and a neighbour off the board reads the zero padding row.
fig.net.stack.label: Layers of the network, from input to output
fig.net.model.label: Model
fig.net.skip: Skip connection: the block adds its own input
fig.net.layer.input.label: Input planes
fig.net.layer.input.detail: The encoder writes the position as {planes} numbers per cell, one plane each, as seen by the side to move. Row 121 is the padding row of zeros. It has no parameters. Class `Encoder`.
fig.net.layer.conv_in.label: Input convolution
fig.net.layer.conv_in.detail: A hex convolution from {planes} planes to 32 channels: gather the cell and its 6 neighbours, multiply by one weight matrix, add a bias, apply ReLU. Class `Network`.
fig.net.layer.block0.label: Residual block 1
fig.net.layer.block0.detail: Two hex convolutions of 32 channels. The block adds its input to the result before the last ReLU, so it only learns a correction: `ReLU(conv2(ReLU(conv1(x))) + x)`. Class `Network`.
fig.net.layer.block1.label: Residual block 2
fig.net.layer.block1.detail: Same structure as block 1, with its own weights. Each block widens the view of a cell by one ring of neighbours per convolution. Class `Network`.
fig.net.layer.block2.label: Residual block 3
fig.net.layer.block2.detail: Same structure as block 1, with its own weights. With every block, a cell combines information from further away on the board. Class `Network`.
fig.net.layer.block3.label: Residual block 4
fig.net.layer.block3.detail: Same structure as block 1, with its own weights. Both heads read the output of this last block. Class `Network`.
fig.net.layer.head_policy.label: Policy head
fig.net.layer.head_policy.detail: A dense layer per cell turns 32 channels into 2 logits: a from-logit and a to-logit. A move scores the from-logit of its start cell plus the to-logit of its target cell; a softmax over the legal moves gives the priors.
fig.net.layer.head_value.label: Value head
fig.net.layer.head_value.detail: The mean over all 121 cells gives 32 numbers. A dense layer of 32 with ReLU follows, then a dense layer with one output per player ({players}) and tanh, which maps each value into −1 to +1.
fig.net.layer.priors.label: Residual priors
fig.net.layer.priors.detail: Two learned numbers add the classical prior: `beta` weighs the distance gain of a move in its logit, `k` weighs the classical evaluation in the value before the tanh. Class `ResidualPriors`.
fig.net.prior.beta: beta = {value}: weight of the distance gain in each move logit
fig.net.prior.k: k = {value}: weight of the classical evaluation in the value
fig.net.gather.title: What one cell gathers
fig.net.gather.desc: A board with one focused cell. Its neighbours on the board are marked; these are the entries that a hex convolution reads for this cell. A cell at the edge has fewer neighbours, and the padding row stands in for the missing ones.
fig.net.gather.padding: Padding row: off the board, all zeros
fig.forward.title: One forward pass, layer by layer
fig.forward.desc: A board heat map follows one real position through the network: first one input plane, then the activation strength of each cell after each layer. A list shows the five legal moves with the highest priors, and one bar per side shows the value on a scale from −1 to +1.
fig.forward.caption: Computed in advance with the scalar Java reference and the shipped expert model, F16 weights widened to F32. Activation strength is the L2 norm over 32 channels; the disc sizes use one scale per position.
fig.forward.step.input: Input: the position as 13 planes of 121 numbers. The board shows the plane “{plane}”; pick another plane below.
fig.forward.step.conv_in: The input convolution turns the 13 numbers of each cell and its neighbours into 32 channels. Larger discs mark cells with a stronger response.
fig.forward.step.block0: Residual block 1: two convolutions, then the block adds its input back. Each convolution lets a cell see one ring of neighbours further.
fig.forward.step.block1: Residual block 2: the same structure with its own weights. Compare the board with block 1 to see which cells change.
fig.forward.step.block2: Residual block 3: each cell now combines information from a wider area of the board than after block 1.
fig.forward.step.block3: Residual block 4: the last layer of the trunk. Both heads read this output.
fig.forward.step.policy: Policy head: from- and to-logits per cell give a prior for each of the {moves} legal moves. The arrows show the five highest.
fig.forward.step.value: Value head: the average over all cells becomes one value per side, {value} for the side to move.
fig.forward.plane.0: Pieces of the side to move
fig.forward.plane.10: Targets of the next player's moves
fig.forward.heat.title: Board after {layer}
fig.forward.heat.desc: Heat map of the board after {layer}: each cell has a disc in one of five sizes; a larger disc means a higher value at that cell.
fig.forward.policy.title: Five highest priors
fig.forward.value.title: Value per side
fig.forward.priors.label: Priors
fig.forward.backends.title: Where the forward pass runs
fig.forward.backends.desc: Dots on a logarithmic axis: measured evaluations per second of the SMALL network for each backend, from the Java scalar reference at 115 positions per second to WebGPU with pipelined batches of 16 at about {n:60000}.
fig.forward.backends.caption: One position per call unless a row names a batch. Java and TornadoVM on an Apple M3 Max; Java figures from a loaded machine are lower bounds. Browser rows measured in Chrome 156, Firefox 157 and Node.js.
fig.forward.backends.note: A GPU pays off only with batches: TornadoVM reaches {n:1968} evaluations per second one at a time and {n:111409} with batches of 256.
fig.mcts.title: MCTS, one simulation at a time
fig.mcts.desc: An icicle tree of the net engine's search in the mid-game position: the root on top, one column per legal move, two levels of replies below. For each simulation the figure marks the selection path, the new leaf and the backup. A table lists prior, visits, mean value and PUCT score of each root move.
fig.mcts.caption: 50 simulations with the expert model at the smallest browser setting: `c` = {n:1.0}, batch 1, no noise. The `c` slider recomputes only the PUCT column for the current state; the tree itself was searched with `c` = {n:1.0}.
fig.mcts.substep.label: Phase
fig.mcts.narration.select: Simulation {k}: selection walks {depth} moves down from the root, starting with {move}, and always takes the move with the highest PUCT score.
fig.mcts.narration.expand: The walk ends after {move}: that position is not in the tree yet, so it becomes a new leaf.
fig.mcts.narration.evaluate: The network rates the new leaf: value {value} for the side to move at the root, plus priors for its {moves} legal moves.
fig.mcts.narration.backup: Each move on the path adds the value of the side that played it. {move} now has {visits} visits and mean value {q}.
fig.mcts.tree.title: Search tree
fig.mcts.tree.desc: Icicle tree: the root bar on top, one column per root move sorted by prior, and two levels of replies below. The path of the current simulation and its new leaf are highlighted; positions not yet expanded are outlined.
fig.mcts.table.caption: Root moves after simulation {k}
fig.mcts.slider.note: The slider only recomputes the PUCT column for this state. The tree was searched with `c` = {n:1.0}.
fig.mcts.final: Choice: {move}, the most visited move, with {visits} of 50 visits
fig.mcts.inset.title: Measured strength by c
fig.mcts.inset.desc: Dot-and-whisker chart of five measurements: the Elo of the net engine against the classical engine for `c` = {n:0.5}, {n:1.0}, {n:1.5}, {n:2.5} and {n:4.0}. The highest value, +338, is at {n:1.0}; the values from {n:0.5} to {n:1.5} overlap.
fig.mcts.inset.caption: Generation-0 SMALL network at 100 simulations against the classical engine at {n:1600} nodes, 100 opening pairs per value. Between {n:0.5} and {n:1.5} the curve is flat.
